concepts.title: A Reluctant Child and the Making of a Dancer
concepts.definition: Kumudini Lakhia recalls that she never wanted to dance as a child; it was her mother who rode crowded trains with an unwilling daughter, and only the pull of film songs turned the child who had begun classes into one who practised willingly four days a week.
concepts.key_idea: Discipline imposed from outside slowly turns into an inner vocation; the guru-shishya framework of classical training carried her even when the child in her resisted.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww137.txt childhood, mother and dance-class passages
question_patterns: why did Kumudini Lakhia not want to dance as a child
what role did the mother play in the dancer's early training
how did the film industry spur the writer's interest in dance
describe the guru-shishya pattern of training described in the essay
what subjects formed the writer's childhood education apart from dance
how does the essay present the struggle behind learning to dance

solution_steps.explain: an unwilling child is taken by local train about forty-five minutes each way to a dance class she did not ask for
imitating a film actor at home persuades the watching mother, and the child keeps attending without complaint
talent grows inside a lattice of parental effort, regular classes and early imitation rather than from a dream of the stage

concepts.title: Technique Must Be Thrown Overboard: Questioning the Form
concepts.definition: The essay repeatedly stages the clash between learned technique and understanding: the young dancer asks why she is gyrating in this way, and her guru finally tells her she has perfected the technique and must now throw it overboard and dance.
concepts.key_idea: Mastery is not the destination; the trained body must become free enough to express meaning, which is why the questioning pupil makes the truer artist.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww137.txt guru's advice and questioning passages
question_patterns: what does the guru mean by perfect the technique and throw it overboard
why did the young dancer begin to question her training
how does the essay connect discipline with a questioning spirit
what was missing in the answer the teacher could not give
explain the phrase to dance means to struggle in the essay
how does questioning a form help an artist internalise it

solution_steps.explain: the pupil wants reasons for each movement while the tradition hands down movement alone
after perfection the guru frees her to dance from understanding rather than from rule
bridges between tradition and creativity are built exactly at this point where discipline meets doubt

concepts.title: Memory, Hunger and the Creative Self
concepts.definition: Two childhood memories organise the essay's inner landscape: the gardener's terrifying revenge for picked guavas, and the mother already dead when the daughter arrived thirty-six hours later, whose hunger the writer says she still mistakes inside herself.
concepts.key_idea: Personal loss and learned fear feed the choreographer's work; the writer treats sensitivity and sentimentality as different powers and chooses the first.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww137.txt gardener episode, mother's death and hunger passages
question_patterns: what lessons did the guava-tree incident teach the writer
how does the essay describe the mother's death and the journey home
why does the writer speak of mistaking different kinds of hunger
distinguish sensitivity from sentimentality as the essay does
how do early memories surface later in the writer's work
what does the window image of the Indian woman suggest in the essay

solution_steps.explain: the seized guava-pickers, the falsely cheerful summons home, the mother dead on arrival after thirty-six hours
bodily, emotional and creative hungers are confused in the writer's own account and visibly feed her choreography
grandmother's training taught her to keep sensitivity while shedding sentimentality, a working rule for art and life

concepts.title: Bridges: Touring, Choreography and Returning Home
concepts.definition: The adult career builds the bridges of the title: seven years abroad, learning folk forms from kummi to ghumar alongside classical training, choreographing works such as Duvidha, Atah Kim and Panch Paras, dancing in more than forty countries, and finally returning to home and family.
concepts.key_idea: The essay's title names the crossings the dancer makes: between tradition and innovation, India and the world, performing and choreographing, public art and private life.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww137.txt tour, choreography, Umrao Jaan note and closing family passage
question_patterns: why is the essay titled Bridges

solution_steps.explain: training at the cultural centre mixes classical and folk forms; touring after the war shows her post-war Germany's desolation and the way stage placement changes a piece
home, marriage, children and friends become another ensemble in which she is no longer a solo performer
every crossing she makes becomes a bridge that carries the past of Kathak into her own new choreography

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the guru's instruction that the dancer should perfect the technique and then throw it overboard, and what it reveals about learning any art.

solution_template.explain: first comes disciplined perfection of technique, then its deliberate abandonment in expression
the writer's demand to know why she gyrates prepares her for that freedom
rules are bridges to be crossed, not walls to live inside; art begins where internalised technique turns into meaning

worked_examples.question_pattern: Justify the title Bridges with reference to the different crossings of Kumudini Lakhia's life described in the essay.

solution_template.explain: childhood resistance to vocation, classical training to creative choreography, India to the world, stage to home
each pair is joined, not chosen: folk forms sit beside kathak, family beside career
the dancer's life is a series of bridges, and the essay narrates their building
